"Now imagine they can do that with every single piece of intellectual property on every platform in real time. That alone should scare the crap out of Americans."

articles.title: Tensions erupt in House hearing as GOP advances anti-socialism resolution while Dems rage: 'Silly season'
articles.summary: House Republicans force Democrats to vote on condemning socialism and capping the Supreme Court at nine justices amid the left's inter-party civil war.
articles.body: House Republicans are teeing up a pair of bills this week to put Democrats on the record about where they stand on their party's socialist insurgency. The House Rules Committee just advanced a resolution to condemn socialism during its Monday meeting, with no Democrats voting in favor of moving it forward. Democrats, in fact, criticized the resolution as a waste of time. Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., called the bill "nonsense" and argued it did little to better the lives of Americans. "So you're concerned about rising gas, or are you concerned about grocery prices? You know, don't worry. Republicans in Congress are passing another non-binding resolution condemning socialism," McGovern said. HOUSE REPUBLICAN AIMS TO PUT DEMOCRATS ON THE RECORD OVER DSA WITH RESOLUTION CONDEMNING SOCIALISM Tensions erupted at one point as Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., clashed with Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., over the definition of socialism. Neguse had attempted to press Steil on whether he would see President Donald Trump trying to take a "20% stake" in Kroger grocery stores as socialism, to which Steil replied he would "want to see the details." "Oh, you'd want to see the details," Neguse yelled as the two men spoke over each other. "You said if the government owns grocery stores, that would be socialist. But if, of course, Donald Trump were to announce an equity stake in a grocery store, well, 'I'd have to really see the details,' because we all know the play." Steil said he would be open to seeing such a proposal if it had a national security imperative, but stated repeatedly that Neguse was posing a hypothetical. At one point, Rules Committee Chairwoman Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., chided Neguse for interrupting Steil. Steil shot back at one point, "Some folks on your side of the aisle would like to have government-run grocery stores. I think that's nuts." "And if the president of the United States announced that the United States government was taking an...equity stake in grocery stores?" Neguse pressed. After more back-and-forth, Steil said, "I think there would need to be a national security rationale for the action. I don't see any in your hypothetical. I don't see a national security focus." Neguse called it a "helpful answer," to which Steil quipped, "It's a hypotherical. So we're entering silly season." A House-wide test known as a "rule vote" on the resolution will take place on Tuesday afternoon, followed finally by a vote on the resolution itself on Tuesday evening, according to a provisional schedule obtained by Fox News Digital. SOCIALISM SURGES AMONG DEMOCRATS AS PARTY LEADERS REJECT DSA AGENDA: ‘PACK OF FOOLS’ It's not uncommon for Democrats on the House Rules Committee to oppose GOP-led measures. But the move is especially stark as Republicans seize on the left's inter-party civil war that has dominated the midterm election cycle. Republicans are capitalizing on that civil war with another measure expected for a vote on Wednesday afternoon, according to that provisional schedule. That vote will be on a constitutional amendment to cap the number of Supreme Court justices at nine. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION Several top progressives, including former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Ed Markey, D-Mass., have called for expanding the Supreme Court to up to 13 seats. House GOP leaders have opted to fast-track that legislation past the House Rules Committee. In exchange, however, it will need two-thirds of the chamber to pass as opposed to a simple majority. CARVILLE UNLOADS ON DSA SOCIALISTS: 'DON'T USE OUR GOD---- NAME' "It's time for the Democrats to pick a side. Stop playing the middle. Be proud of who you are. You were elected to lead, so lead. Have an opinion. We intend to put you on record," House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital. "Do you want to pack the Supreme Court or not? It's really simple. It's a yes or no vote. It's no bigger than that. Two — do you believe in socialism? If you do, you should say it loud and say it proud. I personally don't believe in socialism. I like the fact that we have a democracy, that we have a republic, that we have a free society. And I'm proud to put myself on record." Meanwhile the top Democrat, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., side-stepped a question on whether he supports the anti-socialism resolution on Monday. "I haven't taken a look at that resolution, although it's my understanding that the resolution elevates the so-called SAVE America Act, which is just the 'Suppress the Vote Act.' And I'm not clear how many Democrats are actually gonna support a resolution whose focus is on trying to rig the midterm election by elevating this voter suppression legislation that Donald Trump has been trying to jam down the road to the American people for the last year," he told reporters. JOHNSON SCORES COMMANDING VICTORY IN FIGHT TO RAM SAVE AMERICA ACT THROUGH DEMOCRAT OPPOSITION In addition to condemning socialism, the resolution also hails Republican-led election security bills as "common-sense election integrity measures, including proof of citizenship, photo identification, and database checks." It calls for the "enforcement" of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which has passed the House but has not been taken up in the Senate. Democrats have largely panned that legislation as attempts at voter suppression. Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., said the bill was a bid to "silence political opponents." "Let's scare people with yet another boogeyman and not do anything about it. Not really solve problems, just try to scare people," Scanlon said. Meanwhile, Rep. Nick Langworthy, R-N.Y., pointed out that Democratic socialists were already in power in his own state and warned it could spread elsewhere. And anyone thinks that these ideas are going to stay confined in New York City is sadly mistaken."

articles.title: US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll submits resignation, media reports say
articles.summary: Driscoll’s resignation follows months of tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, US media reports say.
articles.body:
United States Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll has submitted his resignation following months of tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to media reports.

Asked about a Wall Street Journal report on Driscoll’s resignation on Monday, the White House did not deny it.

“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” Spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.

“The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

The Reuters news agency, citing a source familiar with the matter, said it was unclear whether the White House has accepted Driscoll’s resignation.

Driscoll, who is considered close to Vice President JD Vance, is the latest senior official to leave the Pentagon under Hegseth.

The defence secretary fired Army Chief of Staff Randy George in April, while the Army’s commander in Europe and Africa, General Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down in June.

Hegseth has removed several other generals and admirals, including the head of the Navy.

The Pentagon abruptly announced in April that Navy Secretary John Phelan was leaving the job, becoming the first head of a military service to depart during US President Donald Trump’s second term.

articles.title: TSE deepfake: Tribunal define regras para uso de IA nas eleições | G1
articles.standfirst: Tribunal deve definir balizas para enquadrar uso de ferramenta na campanha eleitoral. Caso envolve divulgação de vídeo de Bolsonaro feito com IA na convenção nacional do PL .
articles.summary: O TSE julga o uso de deepfake e inteligência artificial em campanhas, estabelecendo punições para vídeos realistas após polêmica com vídeo de Bolsonaro no PL.
articles.body:
O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) deve definir na noite desta terça-feira (1) um dos temas centrais da eleição deste ano: como deve ser o uso de deepfakes pelas campanhas.

🔎 Deepfake é uma tecnologia de inteligência artificial (IA) usada para criar ou alterar vídeos, áudios e imagens de maneira realista.

Ministros do TSE indicam de forma reservada que a tendência é que a Corte mantenha o veto ao uso de vídeos gerados por IA quando o conteúdo apresentar grau de realismo, seja criando pessoas reais, fictícias ou mortas.

Deve pesar na configuração de deepfake o elevado grau de realismo da manipulação.

Os ministros também devem discutir qual a punição para o candidato ou campanha que usar a ferramenta.

A indicação é de que, além da remoção do vídeo, deve ser aplicada uma multa pelo descumprimento das regras.

As sanções mais graves, como cassação do registro, só devem ser aplicadas nos casos em que ficarem demonstradas a gravidade da conduta, a reincidência e o impacto na disputa.

Também deve ficar expresso que o conteúdo produzido com IA não será permitido apenas por conter rótulo identificando que a peça utilizou a tecnologia.

Na prática, se o plenário confirmar esse entendimento, memes, caricaturas, montagens satíricas, animações e outras representações que não busquem reproduzir a realidade de forma convincente tendem a receber tratamento distinto.

O objetivo do tribunal, segundo interlocutores, é evitar que a vedação alcance manifestações claramente identificáveis como ficção ou humor, concentrando a proibição em conteúdos capazes de induzir o eleitor a erro.

Tribunal Superior Eleitoral aprova regras para uso de inteligência artificial na propaganda eleitoral de 2026 — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Uma resolução eleitoral aprovada neste ano proíbe o uso, para favorecer ou prejudicar candidaturas, de conteúdo sintético em áudio ou vídeo gerado ou manipulado digitalmente para criar, substituir ou alterar a imagem ou a voz de pessoas vivas, falecidas ou fictícias.

O texto prevê a vedação mesmo quando houver autorização da pessoa cuja imagem ou voz tenha sido reproduzida. Algumas campanhas, no entanto, passaram a defender que a regra permitia a chamada "deepfake do bem", que é feita a favor do candidato, por exemplo.

Ministros do TSE, porém, afirmam que a liberação do "deepfake do bem", além de não ser garantia de que o eleitor não será enganado, pode provocar uma enxurrada de ações na Justiça Eleitoral.

A discussão no TSE foi provocada a partir de uma ação da Federação Brasil da Esperança, formada por PT, PCdoB e PV, questionando um vídeo feito por IA que explorava a imagem do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL) exibido na convenção do PL que, confirmou o nome do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) como candidato do partido à Presidência.

Na gravação, a imagem do ex-presidente afirma estar "preso e calado por uma decisão arbitrária", diz que "nenhuma prisão vai calar o sentimento de esperança" e pede que os apoiadores recebam Flávio Bolsonaro "de braços abertos" como candidato à Presidência.

Bolsonaro cumpre atualmente uma pena de 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão. Desde o dia 24 de março deste ano, ele está sob prisão domiciliar humanitária, autorizada por Moraes por um prazo inicial de 90 dias, para que o ex-presidente se recupere de uma broncopneumonia.

"Trata-se, portanto, de expediente que potencializa a propaganda eleitoral antecipada e, simultaneamente, afronta a vedação do uso de inteligência artificial que objetive criar conteúdo sintético para substituir imagem e voz de pessoa viva, além de burlar a restrição judicial imposta ao ex-presidente mediante o emprego de tecnologia de reprodução sintética”, diz a ação.

A campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou ao TSE que o vídeo não violou a legislação eleitoral, porque o uso da tecnologia não foi ocultado e o público foi informado de que não se tratava da presença física, de uma transmissão ao vivo ou de uma gravação autêntica Bolsonaro.

A defesa também sustenta que o material não se enquadra no conceito de deepfake previsto pela Justiça Eleitoral e compara o recurso tecnológico ao uso de máscaras, bonecos e outros instrumentos de representação já utilizados historicamente em campanhas políticas.

Segundo os advogados, houve apenas a criação de um "boneco tecnológico", com avisos e identificação sobre o uso de inteligência artificial, sem indução do público a erro.

Segundo ministros ouvidos pelo blog do Valdo Cruz, no caso específico de Flávio, a tendência é que o plenário se divida em duas correntes sobre a exibição do vídeo durante a convenção do PL:

uma ala defende a aplicação de multa, sob o entendimento de que o material se enquadra como deepfake e poderia levar parte do público a acreditar que a manifestação era autêntica;

outra corrente avalia que não caberia punição, porque o vídeo foi exibido em um evento partidário fechado, destinado principalmente a convencionais e filiados.

Em ações que anteciparam o debate sobre o uso de inteligência artificial nas eleições, o ministro André Mendonça negou, de forma provisória, pedidos da Federação formada por PT/PCdoB/PV para a remoção de conteúdos que usaram IA na produção e indicou sua visão sobre o assunto.

O ministro afirmou que a utilização de montagem ou recurso visual artificial não conduz automaticamente à ilicitude eleitoral.

Para Mendonça, embora o uso de ferramentas de edição e geração audiovisual possa intensificar a carga emocional da mensagem, para retirar o conteúdo do ar “provisoriamente” é preciso demonstrar que o uso da tecnologia “tenha produzido falsidade objetiva, manipulação fraudulenta da realidade ou descontextualização grave apta a induzir o eleitor em erro”.

“Em juízo preliminar, não se constata, com segurança suficiente, que o vídeo tenha descumprido o dever de identificação do uso de inteligência artificial ou que tenha produzido simulação fraudulenta de fala, ato ou conduta específica atribuída falsamente a pessoa determinada (deepfake). Tampouco se evidencia, de plano, que o emprego de IA tenha transformado fatos reais ou debatidos publicamente em fato notoriamente inverídico”, afirmou em uma das ações.

A ministra Estela Aranha discordou de Mendonça e votou pela remoção dos conteúdos nesses casos.

Em outra ação que aborda o uso IA, a ministra afirmou que a configuração de deepfake “independe da demonstração de aptidão concreta da manipulação para induzir o eleitor em erro, assim como não é afastada pela indicação de que o conteúdo foi produzido mediante inteligência artificial”.

Os julgamentos foram interrompidos por pedidos de vista do presidente da Corte, Nunes Marques, até que o plenário enfrentasse o tema.

Em outro caso, também relatado por André Mendonça, o ministro propôs uma tese, segundo a qual a deepfake deve ser considerada uma “representação artificial de pessoa real em situação inexistente mediante imagens dotadas de realismo e verossimilhança suficientes para emular a realidade”.

articles.summary: Tribunal deve consolidar entendimento sobre uso de inteligência artificial nas campanhas. Casos que podem ser afetados envolvem falsos apoios políticos, pesquisas inexistentes e diálogos simulados.
articles.body:
A Justiça Eleitoral tem mais de 50 ações que podem ser impactadas pela decisão do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) que deve fixar nesta terça-feira (1º) o entendimento sobre a proibição de deepfake nas campanhas.

São casos de montagens indicando apoio político, divulgação de resultados de pesquisas que nem existiram e indicavam favoritismo de determinado candidato, diálogos de candidatos simulados e até eleitores fictícios conversando e dando depoimentos a candidatos e jornalistas .

Conteúdos que já geraram milhões de visualizações e alguns casos não havia indicação de que foram gerados por inteligência artificial . Além da remoção do conteúdo, a principal punição tem sido aplicação de multa.

Além do TSE, há casos ao menos na Justiça Eleitoral em São Paulo, Ceará, Bahia, Goiás, Pernambuco e Maranhão.

Diante da preocupação com o uso indevido da inteligência artificial e também com a velocidade de divulgação desses conteúdos falsos, o TSE e diversos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais (TREs) criaram núcleos e conselhos específicos para monitorar as redes sociais, focando no combate às fake news e às deepfakes nas eleições.

As principais campanhas também escalaram assessores para acompanhar a batalha nas redes.

Na prática, memes, caricaturas, montagens satíricas, animações e outras representações que não busquem reproduzir a realidade de forma convincente tendem a receber tratamento distinto.

A resolução eleitoral aprovada neste ano proíbe o uso, para favorecer ou prejudicar candidaturas, de conteúdo sintético em áudio ou vídeo gerado ou manipulado digitalmente para criar, substituir ou alterar a imagem ou a voz de pessoas vivas, falecidas ou fictícias.

O texto prevê a vedação mesmo quando houver autorização da pessoa cuja imagem ou voz tenha sido reproduzida.

Lula em vídeo com música cuja voz foi produzida com auxílio de IA; Flávio Bolsonaro retratado como piloto; Jair Bolsonaro em vídeo sintético exibido na convenção do PL; e Renan Santos em publicação que usa IA em vídeo sobre Daniel Vorcaro — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Em 2024, nas eleições municipais, o TSE já proibiu o uso de deepfake e também exigia que o material feito com inteligência artificial fosse rotulado para informar ao eleitor.

Na época, o uso de conteúdo sexual manipulado por inteligência artificial contra candidatas foi uma das formas mais graves de violência política de gênero e que exigiu atuação da Justiça Eleitoral. Também foram registrados casos de candidatos que "ressuscitaram" padrinhos políticos.

Para as eleições deste ano, as regras foram atualizadas para se adaptar às novidades da ferramenta.

Uma das principais novidades é a proibição para divulgação de conteúdos gerados por IA que utilizem imagem, voz ou manifestação de candidatos ou de pessoas públicas nas 72 horas que antecedem a eleição e nas 24 horas seguintes à votação.

A resolução prevê que os provedores de internet terão que fiscalizar e impedir a divulgação de conteúdos que possam gerar desinformação sobre o processo eleitoral ou possa prejudicar ou favorecer determinada candidatura.

articles.title: VÍDEO: Por que o mandato de senador dura 8 anos, e o de presidente e deputados, 4?  | G1
articles.standfirst: Senadores permanecem oito anos no cargo, e a renovação parcial da Casa busca dar continuidade às decisões políticas; em 2026, 54 das 81 cadeiras estarão em disputa.
articles.summary: Senadores permanecem oito anos no cargo, e a renovação parcial da Casa busca dar continuidade às decisões políticas; em 2026, 54 das 81 cadeiras estarão em disputa.
articles.body:
O mandato de um senador é tão longo que atravessa duas eleições presidenciais. Enquanto o presidente da República é eleito para ficar quatro anos no cargo, os senadores são escolhidos para mandatos de oito anos. E isso não é por acaso. (Entenda no vídeo acima.)

📍Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 vai explicar os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

🔎 A Constituição estabelece que o Senado seja formado por 81 parlamentares , três para cada estado e três para o Distrito Federal, e que cada um tenha mandato de oito anos. A Casa passa por eleições a cada quatro anos, mas somente uma parte das cadeiras é colocada em disputa: alternadamente, um terço e dois terços.

Em 2026, será a vez de renovar dois terços do Senado. Serão eleitos 54 senadores, dois por estado e dois pelo Distrito Federal . As outras 27 cadeiras continuarão ocupadas pelos parlamentares eleitos em 2022, cujos mandatos só terminam em 2031.

➡️O Congresso Nacional é formado por duas Casas: a Câmara dos Deputados e o Senado. De acordo com a Constituição, um projeto de lei aprovado por uma delas precisa ser revisto pela outra, que pode aprovar, rejeitar ou modificar o texto. Caso faça alterações, a proposta volta para a Casa em que começou.

Na prática, o Senado pode funcionar como uma segunda etapa da discussão, dando mais tempo para negociação e reflexão antes que uma proposta avance. Mas ele não é sempre a Casa revisora: isso depende de onde o projeto começou a tramitar.

Não é só a duração do mandato que diferencia o Senado. A Casa também não é renovada por completo em uma única eleição.

É como um time que nunca troca todos os jogadores de uma vez. A cada eleição, alguns mandatos terminam, enquanto outros senadores permanecem no cargo por mais quatro anos. Assim, sempre há parlamentares que já estavam na Casa quando os novos chegam.

Para quem defende o modelo, essa continuidade ajuda a evitar decisões tomadas sob o impacto imediato de uma eleição e dá mais estabilidade ao país. Já os críticos afirmam que os mesmos mecanismos podem tornar mais lentas mudanças que parte da sociedade considera necessárias.

“Historicamente, o Senado era considerado a Casa dos Anciãos, porque é a casa da temperança. Então, o Senado acaba sendo um freio. Você tem critérios de idade mais altos: para a Câmara, a idade é de 21 anos; para o Senado, de 35 anos. No Império, eram 40 anos. E você tem também o critério de tempo”, afirma Leany Lemos, cientista política e membra do Instituto Qualidade de Governo e Políticas para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável.

A diferença de idade mínima permanece na legislação atual: a Constituição exige que candidatos ao Senado tenham ao menos 35 anos, enquanto candidatos a deputado federal podem concorrer a partir dos 21.

“A ideia de ter mandatos descasados, com tempos diferentes e mais longos, é de que você dá mais estabilidade ao longo do tempo”, acrescenta Lemos.

No fim das contas, é por isso que o Senado tem mandatos mais longos e renovação escalonada: a Casa foi desenhada para mudar mais devagar do que outras partes do sistema político, preservando uma parcela de seus integrantes a cada eleição.

Cúpula do Senado Federal e prédio do Congresso Nacional durante o amanhecer. — Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

O debate com candidatos ao Senado por Pernambuco será realizado nesta quarta-feira (2), às 14h, e terá transmissão pelo g1 e pelos perfis do portal no YouTube, TikTok e Instagram. O encontro será mediado pelo jornalista Marcio Bonfim.

Esta será a primeira vez que o g1 realizará uma série de debates com candidatos ao Senado Federal. Os encontros acontecem em setembro nos estúdios da Globo no Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Distrito Federal e Pernambuco, além das afiliadas de Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Ceará e Piauí.

Onde assistir ao debate para o Senado de Pernambuco

O debate com os candidatos ao Senado por Pernambuco poderá ser acompanhado pelo g1 e pelos perfis do portal nas redes sociais:

Quando será o debate para o Senado de Pernambuco?

Os encontros terão como objetivo aprofundar as propostas dos candidatos e priorizar temas de interesse da população. Os participantes ficarão posicionados em uma mesa redonda ao lado do mediador e terão 15 minutos de tempo de fala para administrar ao longo da discussão.

Seis temas serão previamente definidos e comunicados às campanhas antes do debate. A ordem dos assuntos será sorteada antes do início do encontro.

Os candidatos poderão solicitar a palavra dentro das regras estabelecidas, com intervenções de até 1 minuto e 30 segundos por vez. Não serão permitidas intervenções consecutivas do mesmo candidato, que só poderá voltar a falar depois da manifestação de outro participante.

Ao final, todos terão direito a um minuto para as considerações finais.

Os pedidos de direito de resposta serão analisados pela produção e pelo mediador e poderão ser concedidos em casos de ofensa pessoal, conforme as regras previamente acordadas com as campanhas.

Além de Pernambuco, o g1 realizará debates com candidatos ao Senado em outras oito praças durante o mês de setembro:

Mato Grosso : 3 de setembro, às 13h (14h de Brasília);

Mato Grosso do Sul : 4 de setembro, às 13h (14h de Brasília);

Os horários dos debates em Minas Gerais, Distrito Federal, Ceará, Rio de Janeiro, Piauí e São Paulo ainda estão sendo definidos.

A série de debates integra a cobertura especial das Eleições 2026 realizada pela Globo. A iniciativa busca ampliar o espaço para a discussão de propostas e contribuir para que os eleitores conheçam os candidatos ao Senado.

articles.title: Democrats propose counter to GOP’s anti-socialism resolution
articles.summary: Four Democratic lawmakers in the House of Representatives made a move Monday to publicly criticize socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) — as a counter to a Republican resolution that would do the same. The Republican resolution, which was introduced by Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.) and is slated to come to the floor this week,…
articles.body:
Four Democratic lawmakers in the House of Representatives made a move Monday to publicly criticize socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) — as a counter to a Republican resolution that would do the same.

The Republican resolution , which was introduced by Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.) and is slated to come to the floor this week, condemns socialism and DSA policy positions, like abolishing prisons and allowing noncitizens to vote.

It also includes a call for “enactment of the SAVE America Act,” President Trump’s long-sought bill that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and photo ID to cast a ballot. That bill has failed to pass the Senate multiple times, but has remained a top priority for Trump and many in his base.

The proposed Democratic amendment to that resolution also denounces socialism, though using different language. The authors list the failures of socialism in other nations and several controversial DSA positions, like abolishing capitalism and the Armed Forces, and call the DSA’s ideology “incompatible with American values and the United States Constitution.” It also strips out the provision related to the SAVE America Act.

The GOP resolution advanced out of the House Rules Committee without allowing a vote on the amdnment. But the Democratic backers said the goal of the proposal was about showing voters Republicans aren’t being sincere.

“I mean, it’s really trying to show the Republicans are not serious about wanting to do that, right?” Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fl.) told The Hill Monday night. “This is just political games.”

Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) said the socialism debate is not what Congress should be focused on, but that if Republicans are going to make hay, she also wants to ensure that it’s “serious.”

“To put the SAVE Act in there, it actually dilutes the power of what this socialism resolution is and and should be attempting to do,” Scholten told The Hill. “So you know our amendment just simply attempts to expose this fraudulent, insincere attempt by Republicans and say, ‘hey, if you guys really want to have a vote on socialism, let’s have it, right?’ And separate out these two issues.”

“If the Republican leadership truly wants to have a conversation about socialism, then let’s have the real conversation we need to have about it,” Scholten said. “I’m open to having that conversation, but you know not with this watered down insincere version that includes the Save Act, which is deeply unpopular with the American people.”

Republicans have been making the fight against socialism a hallmark of their midterm message , casting the democratic socialists and progressives who have scored recent primary wins as extreme and seeking to tie the rest of the party to its most far-left members.

Some Democrats, meanwhile, have been sounding the alarm about the DSA for months out of concern that its candidates could harm their midterm prospects and cost them the battleground districts that will decide the House.

articles.title: Dan Driscoll: US army secretary resigns after months of tension
articles.summary: Dan Driscoll, the youngest-ever army secretary, was about 18 months into his post.
articles.body:
US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation after about 18 months in the role.

His departure was confirmed by CBS, the BBC's US media partner, which reported it came after months of conflict between him and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The youngest-ever army secretary has often been referred to as President Donald Trump's "drone guy".

Driscoll, 41, has been "highly effective" in advancing Trump's agenda "to Make America Strong Again" and provided "outstanding leadership" during military operations, the White House said in a statement given to CBS.

The BBC has contacted the White House, Pentagon and Army for comment.

Driscoll is the latest in a string of recent high-profile military leaders to depart, including Navy Secretary John Phelan who abruptly quit in April .

Other notable departures include Army Chief of Staff Randy George, Army Gen David Hodne and Maj Gen William Green.

Since entering the Pentagon, Hegseth has fired more than a dozen senior military officers, including the chief of naval operations and the Air Force's vice-chief of staff.

The details of the behind-the-scenes friction between Driscoll and Hegseth are unclear but CBS notes that the army secretary is good friends with George, who was reportedly asked by Hegseth to resign.

The post of army secretary is the top civilian leader of the US Army, directing active duty troops, along with the National Guard and reserve soldiers.

Driscoll previously served in the Army and was an officer in 2007 before leading a cavalry platoon and deploying to Iraq for several months in 2009.

As army secretary, Driscoll became known as Trump's "drone guy" due to his embrace of emerging battlefield technologies.

He took on a leading role last year in talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, taking on foreign trips and meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

He's also a close ally and friend of Vice-President JD Vance, whom he met at Yale Law School.

During his tenure as head of the US Army, he was a key figure in Trump's deployment of the National Guard to US cities.

He also took over the role of acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

articles.title: Trump calls for federal tax incentives to benefit TV and movie industry
articles.summary: The proposal was quickly embraced by Democrats, particularly in California, who have otherwise been critical of the president.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Monday called for bipartisan tax incentives to help a domestic TV and movie industry that has seen large chunks of its business move overseas in recent years. Trump wrote on Truth Social that meetings were “being set up with the Leaders of both Parties in order to get this done.” “It should be Bipartisan, especially since so much money is being lost in California, and other largely Blue States,” he wrote. “I am going to suggest that Republicans and Democrats get together, and immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America.” Trump indicated that his call to help Hollywood — an industry that Republicans often rail against and one that resides in solidly blue California — was influenced in part by actor Jon Voight, who was a 2024 campaign surrogate for him. Voight, whom Trump has called his “Hollywood ambassador,” has helped shape Trump’s policy toward the entertainment industry during his second term. In May 2025, Trump met with Voight before he proposed tariffs on films produced overseas. Voight did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night. Trump’s Truth Social post drew immediate support from Democrats who are usually critical of him and his administration’s policies. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., a frequent Trump target, said he was in “strong agreement” with Trump on this one. “Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we’ve lost to other countries,” Schiff wrote on X. “Let’s work together — Republicans and Democrats — to get this done, and bring the movie magic back to America.” Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Calif., praised the proposed measure and called for swift passage. “For more than a year I’ve been sitting down with Jon Voight, Congressional colleagues, the unions, studios, and producers to build the case for a national film and television tax credit,” Friedman said in a statement. “There’s no reason Canada, the UK, or Australia should be taking our jobs. We still have the best crews on the planet. It’s time we made it possible for them to stay where they belong: in America.” Friedman said last September that the proposed tariffs on foreign films were recognition from Trump that the U.S. was losing its domestic film and TV industry but that the path forward was a tax credit, not tariffs. Trump’s announcement Monday was also embraced by the industry itself. Charles Rivkin, the CEO of the Motion Picture Association, the trade group representing major film studios in the U.S., said in a statement that the group applauded Trump’s support for tax incentives. “For over a century, American studios, casts, and crews have produced the films and series that the world wants to see. A federal incentive would be a landmark step toward bringing more production to local communities in all 50 states, strengthening our nation’s economy, and making our country a more competitive place to produce, create, and tell great stories,” Rivkin said in his statement. While Trump did not lay out any financial details in his post, he predicted that the money spent on the tax incentives “will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers.”

articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has been a key figure in a push to release files linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein in the last few years, read off over a dozen names of what he said were “Epstein coconspirators” on Monday.

“On the House floor tonight, I read the names of several Epstein coconspirators who should be investigated and prosecuted,” Massie said in a Monday night post on the social platform X.

“I also began collecting 218 signatures for the discharge petition to force a vote on Epstein Files Transparency Act II,” he added.

Massie’s post included a clip of himself on the House floor, in which he said it had “been a year since the president signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act,” referencing legislation he spearheaded alongside Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) last year that resulted in the release of some files linked to Epstein.

“And the government continues to withhold over three million files. That’s why we’ve introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, to bring the fight to the state courts, accountability to the Department of Justice and closure for survivors. We want perpetrators of these crimes to be investigated and prosecuted,” he added.

Massie then began to list off names, including Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, and billionaire retail mogul Les Wexner.

The former prince was accused of sexual abuse by Virginia Giuffre, who also alleged that the abuse occurred after Epstein trafficked her. Mountbatten-Windsor has denied that he ever met Giuffre.

In February, Wexner denied firsthand knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activity during a deposition with the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. Wexner had employed Epstein as a financial manager in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Massie said in an earlier post on X Monday that the Epstein Files Transparency Act II “gives state [attorneys general] access to Epstein files required to prosecute perpetrators under state law, and makes it easier for survivors to sue to get their files.”

articles.title: White House provides details on Venezuela oil deal Trump announced
articles.summary: The deal gives the Pentagon a 35% ownership stake in the private company being created, and the State Department will get a guarantee to purchase 20% of the output at cost.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The White House on Monday said it’s partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners as part of President Donald Trump’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry, setting up a deal that will give the Pentagon a stake over roughly a fifth of the country’s vast oil reserves. The Trump administration released more details about the agreement on Monday night, days after Trump announced what he described as the biggest oil deal in history. The sweeping deal has been met with skepticism from analysts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela’s production, but Trump and his aides are pitching it as a chance to develop a new oil giant in the Western Hemisphere. As part of the deal, the U.S. is creating a private company as part of a joint venture with NABEP — a detail the White House withheld for days. NABEP, owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, is already the second-largest operator in Venezuela behind Chevron. Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, is giving the company 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. Many of those fields were previously owned by Russian or Chinese firms, the White House said. The deal will give the Pentagon a 35% ownership stake in the company, and the State Department will get a guarantee to purchase 20% of the output at cost, the White House disclosed Monday. Betancourt’s company has agreed to put up $100 billion in new oil infrastructure. In a statement Monday, Betancourt said Venezuela is “blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential,” adding that the deal will “unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans.” The company said Betancourt had been involved in the Venezuelan oil industry for more than 15 years and said the company has more than 5,000 employees and more than 10,000 contractors. Trump has been pushing to boost oil production in Venezuela since the January military mission that captured then-President Nicolás Maduro on federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges. The White House said the deal would be “at zero cost” to the U.S. and said the government would have veto power on board members — the majority of whom would be U.S. citizens. “NABEP will have reputable U.S. auditors, lawyers, and advisers and the U.S. government’s agreement with NABEP is governed by U.S. law and is subject to the jurisdiction of U.S. courts,” the White House said in a fact sheet about the deal. Former U.S. government energy advisers have cautioned that the deal comes with political risk, since future administrations in Venezuela or the United States could challenge the deal. Even if the agreement holds, analysts say it could take years to turn around Venezuela’s dilapidated energy sector. Even Trump, who says the plan will reduce gas prices, acknowledged Monday that Americans won’t see change right away. Asked about it at the White House, Trump said “it could be a little bit” for prices to fall, though he played down analyst predictions that it could take years. “If it was two years, you know, that’s a short period of time,” he said. Rodríguez has spoken in favor of the deal, describing it as a chance to modernize Venezuela’s oil industry and accelerate its revival. Facing criticism that the deal cedes Venezuelan resources to the U.S., Rodríguez insisted her country’s sovereignty remains secure. Lawmakers on Capitol Hill said they were looking for more information about the agreement. Rep. Rick Crawford, the Republican chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, said he wanted to hear details from the Trump administration “hopefully sooner rather than later.” Sen. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said a deal that uses the military to boost a private oil venture should be rejected and said he wanted a full accounting of the legal authority for the agreement. “President Trump’s effort to turn the U.S. military into an investor in Venezuelan oil is a blatant abuse of power and taxpayer dollars,” Reed said in a statement. Trump plans to meet Tuesday with a group of large and small oil refiners to discuss ways to increase America’s capacity to refine oil into gasoline. The meeting occurs as the Iran war has driven prices at the pump to a national average of $4.08, a 28% increase over the past year, according to AAA. The White House has said that increasing the number of refineries and expanding the capacity at existing facilities would eventually reduce prices for consumers. The administration also sees the need for more refineries to process oil from Venezuela. Also attending the meeting will be Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Jarrod Agen, the director of the White House National Energy Dominance Council.

articles.title: El-Sayed on Vance ‘evil’ remark: ‘What’s evil is corrupting yourself’
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Monday shot back at Vice President Vance’s comment about him being “very, very evil.” Earlier Monday, Vice President Vance went after El-Sayed at a rally in Detroit, calling him “evil.” “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States…
articles.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Monday shot back at Vice President Vance’s comment about him being “very, very evil.”

Earlier Monday, Vice President Vance went after El-Sayed at a rally in Detroit, calling him “evil.”

“There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today,” Vance said.

In an interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins Monday night, El-Sayed responded to Vance’s comments by seemingly taking a dig at the latter’s political shift toward President Trump in the last decade.

“Well, let me tell you what’s evil,” El-Sayed said when Collins asked about Vance’s remarks. “Evil is the idea of starting wars when there’s peace. Evil is the idea of stripping away people’s healthcare when they absolutely have no other option. What’s evil is to do that, so that you can pass a tax cut for billionaires.”

“What’s evil is putting a data center that people don’t want in their backyard, to spite them. What’s evil is corrupting yourself because you want a little bit more power,” he added.

El-Sayed supports policies like the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), drawing down U.S. financial support for Israel and Medicare for All. He won his primary earlier this month amid a wave of progressive candidates that notched primary wins in races against establishment figures.

El-Sayed is facing off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) for Sen. Gary Peters’s (D-Mich.) seat in November in a key battleground state that former President Joe Biden won in 2020 and President Trump won in 2024. However, Rogers may be facing an uphill political battle as issues like the Iran war, concerns about the economy and Trump’s slumping approval numbers dog the GOP.

articles.title: Get right out of town
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson faces a tricky week as Republicans push a socialism vote and the SAVE America Act before Members flee to campaign.
articles.body: The House of Representatives is back in town after not voting since July 23. But the House is only back for less than a week. And the Senate doesn’t even return until Monday, September 14. The first day of school, this is not. House members descending on the Capitol this week – then abandoning Washington for Labor Day is kind of like the third and final preseason game in the NFL. THE WILL OF 100: TRUMP’S SAVE AMERICA ACT SIDELINED AFTER SENATE UNANIMOUSLY AGREED TO AUGUST EXIT Lots of fans show up for the first game of the NFL preseason. It’s usually a nice – if sweltering – August night. Not some bone-shivering chill in Cleveland with a foot of snow on the ground in mid-December. There’s anticipation. The first look at the new team. The first tailgate. First-string players and highly touted draft picks even play a series or two. But by the third preseason game, few want to be there. The die is cast for the roster spots. Players are cut. Even the most robust fans only show up for a quarter or two. In the NFL, everyone is waiting for the regular season to begin in a few weeks. That’s kind of where things are now in the House. Congress has tackled most of its business for the year. The highly-touted GOP "Reconciliation 3.0" likely falls by the wayside. Lawmakers even tucked into bed the usual autumn drama surrounding a possible government shutdown. The chances of a repeat following last year’s 43-day shutdown saga dissipated in early August when the Senate approved an interim, bipartisan bill which will fund the government through December 11. The House votes on that bill Tuesday. Everyone on Capitol Hill is now waiting for the regular season to begin. That’s what awaits the body politic following the midterm elections in November. And most members don’t even want to linger in Washington right now. As fast as they came to Washington, they wanted to skate out of town to campaign. That’s why attendance might be sparse over the next few days. The House had 384 members present for one non-controversial measure Monday night. A second vote recorded 388 members present. Those attendance figures could slide if the House returns to Washington in mid-September – as the schedule dictates. Especially among those who either lost their primaries or are retiring. In fact, Fox is told that some members in both camps have even considered resigning early. Imagine what that could do to the narrow Republican majority. TRUMP DEMAND PUTS VULNERABLE REPUBLICANS IN IMPOSSIBLE SPOT AHEAD OF MIDTERMS So, will the House stick it out this week, go home and come back in a few weeks? "Are we going to be here the entire period?" yours truly asked House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. "We’re going to be here this week and then we're going to come back in a couple weeks?" "Well, it’s on the schedule," Johnson replied. That’s a schedule which the House Republican leadership etched out last December – on the heels of that epic government shutdown. Who could have anticipated that government funding could work out so easily this time around. So what’s on the agenda? Republicans plan a vote on a resolution to get Democrats on the record of either supporting socialism or democracy. In other words, the GOP wants Democrats to put their voting cards where their policies are. "They want to abolish things like the U.S. Supreme Court. The United States Senate," said Rep. Jeff Crank R-Colo. Republicans hope to compel Democrats to either accept or reject progressive, left-wing ideologies. "We need to see where Democrats stand on this because the American people are rejecting it," said Rep. Tom Tiffany R-Wis., on Fox. "They're going to try to distance themselves as much as they can," said Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla. "But the fact is that's where the Democratic Party is going. That's where the energy of the Democratic Party is going." This is what’s described in Congress as a "gotcha" vote. Republicans will dare Democrats to vote no. And if they do, the GOP will deploy that vote against vulnerable Democrats in campaign ads this fall. Some Democrats could vote to reject any relationship with socialism. In fact, the vote could give those Democrats a gift to say they’re opposed to socialists in the Democratic Party. But Republicans ensconced a measure in the resolution which could oblige Democrats to vote no. The measure includes the SAVE America Act. That’s the hallmark of the GOP’s agenda. It requires proof of citizenship for voting. Most Democrats view the SAVE America Act as a poison pill. So Democrats could vote nay. And some Republicans will still say "gotcha" if they oppose it. "The resolution elevates the so-called Save America Act, which is just the ‘suppress the vote act,’ said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries D-N.Y. "I'm not clear how many Democrats are actually going to support a resolution whose focus is on trying to rig the midterm election by elevating this voter suppression legislation that Donald Trump has been trying to jam down the throats of the American people for the last year." The House could also wrestle with a resolution to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C. He admitted to inappropriate conduct around female aides and dropped his reelection bid. There could be an effort to expel Rep. Cory Mills R-Fla. He faces allegations of financial misconduct and alleged assault of a woman at his apartment last year. But Mills lost his primary. Then there is Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio. The Ohio Republican faces allegations of spousal and child abuse. Republicans implored Miller to drop his reelection bid. But Miller doubled down, saying the allegations are false. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Johnson says he supports Miller’s "reelection." He contends the House shouldn’t take action until the Ethics Committee completes its inquiry. "He has been a great Member of Congress," said Johnson of Miller. "He has some personal issues he’s still working through." But it’s possible Democrats – and even some Republicans – could engineer a special resolution to expel or otherwise punish Miller. Johnson and the GOP leadership want nothing to do with that. So the solution? Get lawmakers off Capitol Hill and back into their districts. Fast. Yes, it’s unclear what the Senate may address when it returns in a few weeks. But House Republicans are more concerned with clinging to their narrow majority in November. So recessing until after the election could prove to be the safest political tactic for Republicans. Don’t be surprised if the House leaves Washington until November in the next few days. articles.title: Trump creates new headache for GOP with call for FCC to crack down on NBC, Welker
articles.summary: President Trump’s call on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to crack down on NBC’s “Meet the Press” after host Kristen Welker said the president has a “mixed record” on endorsements this year is a new political headache for GOP lawmakers and candidates. Republicans weathered a public backlash last year when the FCC threatened it could pursue…
articles.body:
President Trump’s call on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to crack down on NBC’s “Meet the Press” after host Kristen Welker said the president has a “mixed record” on endorsements this year is a new political headache for GOP lawmakers and candidates.

Republicans weathered a public backlash last year when the FCC threatened it could pursue “remedies” if ABC didn’t punish late-night host Jimmy Kimmel after he quipped that the “kid who killed Charlie Kirk” was a member of the “MAGA gang.”

Some political experts say Trump is putting Republicans in a tough position by calling on the FCC to punish Welker — one of the highest profile journalists in Washington — over comments that appeared to be an editorial assessment of Trump’s record.

“It’s complete overreach on Trump’s part. People comment on politicians all the time and he just seems to go after anybody who disagrees with him,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution’s governance studies program.

“The public is tired of Trump’s revenge tour against anybody who disagrees with him. It’s hard to know how the FCC will respond, but the law clearly protects freedom of expression so if the FCC does punish NBC, I would expect there to be litigation,” he said.

While GOP lawmakers agreed that Kimmel’s comments crossed the line, they warned that pursuing regulatory penalties against a major broadcast network because of the controversial comments of a comedian risked regulating speech.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, warned a year ago that FCC Chair Brendan Carr’s threat to take action against ABC sounded like something “right out of Goodfellas” — the classic mob movie — and “dangerous as hell.”

The Walt Disney Company and ABC last month filed a lawsuit against the FCC, arguing that the Trump administration violated its rights by launching an early review of its broadcast licenses in response to its content.

The FCC ordered the review amid an investigation into Disney about its diversity, equity and inclusion policies.

Now Trump has threatened to reanimate that controversy by calling on the FCC to rebuke or punish Welker after she claimed he had a “mixed record” in picking GOP primary winners, even though Trump has compiled a 96 percent winning record in primaries this year, according to Ballotpedia.

Trump said Welker “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment” because of what he called her “purposeful inaccuracy.”

“The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” he wrote on Truth Social.

NBC has backed up its star Sunday morning host.

GOP strategists say Trump still has a strong grip on the Republican Party, but they warn it is slipping and they fear his poor numbers with independent voters could rub off on Republican incumbents running in swing states, even those that are GOP-leaning swing states.

“He’s losing it a little bit when he picks really flawed people,” said a Republican strategist, who requested anonymity to discuss Trump’s support of several Republicans who lost in this year’s gubernatorial primaries.

While Trump boasts a 100 percent record picking winners in Senate Republican primary contests this election cycle, several of his high-profile gubernatorial picks have lost.

They include Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa), MyPillow founder Mike Lindell and South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette.

In House Republican primaries, GOP candidate Catalina Lauf and Rep. Cory Mills (Fla.) lost in Florida, while Republican challenger Amir Hassan lost in Michigan’s 8th District and Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lost in Tennessee’s 5th District.

The GOP strategist argued Lindell and Ogles are flawed candidates that Trump couldn’t carry over the finish line, while the source praised Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who won her primary runoff with Trump’s backing, as a more “normal” candidate.

The Republican strategist said Trump is courting another major controversy right before the election by calling on the FCC to punish NBC because of Welker’s statement, which she made during a promotional appearance on NBC’s local Washington, D.C., affiliate.

“If Brendan were to do anything, that would be a bridge too far. It would clearly be illegal and he’d be slapped down by a court as soon as the opportunity arose,” the strategist warned.

The FCC’s website states that it has limited power under the First Amendment to restrict or ban speech and that the Communications Act states the commission does not have the power to interfere with the right of free speech by means of broadcast communication.

Trump’s outburst against Welker, however, has put more of a spotlight on his slipping poll numbers with GOP voters. While the president remains very popular with Republicans, his numbers have come down since the start of his second term.

Whit Ayres, a prominent Republican pollster, said Trump’s numbers are softening with GOP voters but are still strong enough to help candidates in competitive primaries.

“The president’s endorsement in Republican primaries is still a very powerful element,” he said.

But Trump’s popularity with Republicans has been tested by broad public dissatisfaction over costs and the war with Iran, which has dragged on for six months.

“It’s down from sky-high levels to only high levels,” Ayres said of Trump’s poll numbers with Republicans.

“The challenge is his rating in a general election electorate, not a Republican primary,” he added.

A new University of Massachusetts Amherst poll conducted of a thousand respondents across the country from Aug. 21-26 found that 4 in 5 Americans say that food and gas prices have increased under Trump and two-thirds of U.S. adults disapprove of his handling of the Iran war.

The poll found that 27 percent of Republican respondents said Trump has performed somewhat or much worse than they expected.

Trump, however, flexed his political muscle in GOP primaries earlier this year when he backed challengers who defeated high-profile Republican incumbents — including GOP Rep. Thomas Massie in Kentucky, and Republican Sens. Bill Cassidy in Louisiana and John Cornyn in Texas.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and other GOP senators had lobbied Trump to back Cornyn over Ken Paxton, the Lone Star State’s attorney general, who is now trailing in polls to Texas state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate.

Paxton told Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing” that his own polls show him performing better against Talarico but acknowledged “we definitely have a close race.”

Talarico leads by an average of nearly 2 percentage points, according to a compilation of recent polls by RealClearPolitics.

Trump on Sunday touted his endorsement as “without question, the strongest Endorsement in the History of Politics.”

He cited his support for Graham in the South Carolina Senate race and candidate Mike Mazzei in the Republican gubernatorial primary in Oklahoma. Mazzei, a businessman, narrowly beat Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond.

articles.title: New turbulence upends stability of Iran war for Trump
articles.summary: There is new turbulence in the war in Iran — but the pressing question is whether any of it will change the underlying realities of the six-month conflict. The latest dramatic development was an exchange of fire late Sunday in which the United States first attacked two Iranian rocket launchers that were reportedly seeking to deploy new…
articles.body:
There is new turbulence in the war in Iran — but the pressing question is whether any of it will change the underlying realities of the six-month conflict.

The latest dramatic development was an exchange of fire late Sunday in which the United States first attacked two Iranian rocket launchers that were reportedly seeking to deploy new mines in the vital Strait of Hormuz.

Iran responded by firing several missiles toward U.S. forces deployed in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, though the counterstrikes appear to have been largely intercepted.

It does not look like a slide back toward full-scale war is imminent, even amid the volatility.

On Monday morning, President Trump again lashed out at Iran , which he contended was “officially a Failed Nation” with leadership “in total disarray.”

But social media posts alone don’t change the state of a conflict that has endured far longer than Trump’s initial projections and looks sure to be an electoral burden on Republicans in November’s midterm elections.

Even the relatively modest scale of the newest exchanges of fire caused the price of benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude oil to rise ​more than 3 percent at one point on Monday. The price hovered around $86 per barrel, roughly $20 up from prewar levels.

Meanwhile, polls show the American public disapproving of Trump’s handling of Iran by almost 2 to 1.

Still, it’s always possible that public perception could shift if the war were perceived to be moving onto a different, more positive trajectory for the U.S.

Some people think it might — and not all of them are pro-Trump.

Brett McGurk, the controversial foreign policy adviser who has served presidents of both parties and is now a CNN analyst, wrote on Sunday that “the status quo — perhaps for the first time since the war began — now favors Washington, not Tehran.”

The case made by McGurk — and other optimists for the American side — has several components.

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has increased, even though there are very divergent estimates of the scale of the change. Even a modest increase holds out the prospect of loosening Iran’s main point of strategic leverage, however.

Then there is the question of whether Trump’s ramping up of economic pressure will bite hard enough to change attitudes in Tehran.

While most experts believe this approach isn’t a fix in the very short term, they don’t think it’s guaranteed to fail either.

“I am guessing that the hope is that if the regime cannot pay its internal security forces, you will then see a separation between the fellow travelers and the true believers — and you could see further discontent within the general population,” Robert Wilkie, who served as secretary of Veterans Affairs during the first Trump administration, told this column.

Finally, those who see a changing tide note some signs of division within the Iranian leadership. Some top figures in Tehran, including President Masoud Pezeshkian, have seemed at pains to keep diplomatic routes open. Hardliners, concentrated around Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, generally characterize the negotiations as American trickery to create an interlude before all-out war resumes.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on social media Friday that “putting diplomacy back on track isn’t impossible” — though he also noted, “It hinges on U.S. understanding of one simple fact: pressure doesn’t work.”

But other experts are deeply skeptical that there’s a sea change coming in the conflict anytime soon.

Many note the Islamic Republic is in a fight for its survival, that it has been emboldened by its ability to endure the initial U.S.-Israeli military assault that began Feb. 28 and that leaders in Tehran are well aware of the political dynamics pressing in on Trump and the GOP.

Aaron David Miller, who served in the State Department for decades, with a focus on the Middle East, contended that the easing of traffic restrictions in the Strait and the economic blockade “have persuaded some in the administration — maybe Trump — that he actually is winning; that he will break the Iranian economy, oil will get through the straits and Iran will change.”

But Miller, now a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, argued that such optimism would be “a mistake.”

“Both parties think time is on their side, both parties think they have the capability for escalation, and both parties seem willing to absorb the economic and political pain,” he added.

Trita Parsi, the Iranian-born executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, saw no breakthrough imminent for either side but asserted it was the U.S. that was in a state of “strategic disarray.”

Parsi argued that the Trump administration keeps toggling between different approaches, none of which appears to be delivering American objectives.

He expressed concern that the de facto U.S. policy was becoming one of maintaining some level of intermittent military attacks on Iran for the long term — an approach he noted would be unpopular with the public.

“The U.S. will never declare it is in a forever war,” he said. “But if your strategy becomes that you have to periodically bomb this country, you are saying you do not have a strategy to resolve this.”

Miller, the former State Department figure, was equally circumspect about the overall conflict.

“No matter how this ends, it’s just another round in a historic half-century battle between the Islamic Republic and the U.S.,” he said. “There are no transformative endings, no Hollywood endings.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Democratic incumbents in Massachusetts hope to defy primary push for generational change
articles.summary: A fierce primary fight from the left risks toppling an eighth House Democrat this cycle: Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.). Lynch, 71, is running for a 14th term in Massachusetts’s 8th Congressional District against 39-year-old lawyer Patrick Roath for the Boston-area seat on Tuesday. Roath has ripped Lynch over votes on immigration, healthcare and abortion, while…
articles.body:
A fierce primary fight from the left risks toppling an eighth House Democrat this cycle: Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.).

Lynch, 71, is running for a 14th term in Massachusetts’s 8th Congressional District against 39-year-old lawyer Patrick Roath for the Boston-area seat on Tuesday. Roath has ripped Lynch over votes on immigration, healthcare and abortion, while the incumbent has pointed to his decades of experience and legislative accomplishments for the district.

This House race, however, is not the only Massachusetts contest where an incumbent faces a fierce primary challenge. Rep. Richard Neal (D) and Sen. Ed Markey (D) are both facing off against younger challengers as the party grapples with an antiestablishment mood and widespread calls for generational change.

“What’s telling is that you have seen some outside spending that has come in to support Roath,” explained Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley, adding “you don’t see that” for the primary challenger vying for Neal’s seat in the 1st District.

Roath, who served as an aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick (D), has centered his campaign around generational change and voiced frustration over the congressman’s votes against former President Obama’s signature healthcare package in 2010 and for the Laken Riley Act.

“Our team has knocked tens of thousands of doors, and we’re feeling the energy with two days left,” Roath — who is backed by Patrick as well as David Hogg’s Leaders We Deserve grassroots organization — told The Hill in a statement. “Even people who have supported Stephen Lynch for two decades are ready for change.”

Meanwhile, 39-year-old Jeromie Whalen is vying to oust 77-year-old Neal, who has represented western Massachusetts in the House since 1989.

Whalen told The Hill he is running because of corporate influence in elections, though the high school teacher has regularly spoken about how he’s half the congressman’s age.

“You can’t advocate for lower utility bills when you’re taking money from Eversource,” he said. “You can’t advocate truly on behalf of affordable housing when Blackstone, the world’s largest landlord, is one of your biggest donors.”

Lynch and Neal have both touted their triumphs in the district as well as their backgrounds and decades of experience on Capitol Hill through their campaigns.

“My ability to successfully represent the hardworking families of this district comes from the fact that my family was one of those hardworking families in this district,” Lynch said during a recent candidate forum. He has also pointed to his support for the DREAM Act when it was initially politically unpopular.

Neal is the ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee and maintains a clear fundraising advantage over Whalen, raising $2.2 million to date. His challenger has raised just more than $330,000 in the same time period.

“Billions of dollars have come back to the people of western and central Massachusetts,” Neal said during the pair’s only debate . “There has not been a life in central and western Massachusetts that has not had a positive impact because of the efforts that I’ve made. I’ve been here. I have fought [President] Trump.”

Skelley suggested that while Lynch is seen as the favorite heading into Tuesday, Roath has notably out-fundraised the congressman and could upset the incumbent.

“We have seen some Democrats struggle in primaries after, say, voting in favor of the Laken Riley Act, which Lynch did do,” the DDHQ chief elections analyst said.

The marquee Senate race in the state spotlights the same conversations around age, but with a twist. Rep. Seth Moulton (D), 47, is mounting a longshot challenge against Markey for the progressive senator’s seat — from his right.

“Moulton is arguably the wrong candidate at the right time,” Skelley said, adding that “another young primary challenger with his kind of elected credentials might have been able to really threaten Markey.”

Though the 10-term House Democrat has sought to position himself as a progressive, Markey has notched key support from the party’s left flank, including Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) as well as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). The incumbent also sponsored the Green New Deal.

Moulton has also faced flak for comments he made after the 2024 election suggesting transgender women and girls shouldn’t play in sports that align with their gender. He since apologized for the comments.

articles.title: Democrats, shook by woke and Trump, make case they’re the normal ones
articles.summary: The 2028 Democratic presidential primary is shaping up as a contest over who can seem the most reasonable. Prospective candidates are imploring their party to be normal, while battling among one another over who is the most normal of all. California Gov. Gavin Newsom is making an appeal to his party to become more “culturally normal,”…
articles.body:
The 2028 Democratic presidential primary is shaping up as a contest over who can seem the most reasonable.

Prospective candidates are imploring their party to be normal, while battling among one another over who is the most normal of all.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is making an appeal to his party to become more “culturally normal,” while Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has urged his fellow Democrats to “talk like a normal human being.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has said that those in her party need to speak in ways that aren’t reminiscent of “the faculty lounge,” a nod to the pundit class.

It all looks like a pushback against “woke,” which many Democrats blame for their losses in 2024.

And it’s also an attempt to ride out what Democrats believe is the backlash forming against what they see as the absurdities of the Trump 2.0 era in Washington, D.C. and the country at large.

“As we look forward, and this is most relevant in the presidential primary process, the question general election voters will ask is, ‘Which of these candidates seems reasonable to me? And which one of them is less crazy?’” said Matt Bennett, the executive vice president for public affairs at Third Way, the moderate think tank.

“And somehow Democrats have come up on the losing side of that twice and we can’t let that happen again,” Bennett added, referring to the two wins by Trump in 2016 and 2024.

Since the 2024 election, Democrats have wrestled with how they lost their way with the electorate, particularly the working class and Black and Hispanic voters, who were traditionally part of their coalition, but spurned Vice President Kamala Harris for Trump.

In election post-mortems since then, Democrats have concluded that they were too wedded to cultural politics and a vocabulary that put off many voters, from pronouns to terms including “Latinx.” That turned off a key segment of voters, a number of Democrats now believe.

Earlier this month, even Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who will own the progressive lane of the 2028 presidential contest if she becomes a candidate, laughed when she quoted a New York City councilman saying, “Woke 1 was crazy.”

It was a shift of sorts for Ocasio-Cortez and a nod that the left flank may have overstepped in recent years, particularly in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Democrats are looking back not only at the pronouns, but the calls to “defund the police,” and a broader embrace of “cancel culture.”

More recently, some centrist Democrats have become increasingly worried about the Democratic Socialists who have won in a string of primaries.

The battlelines have focused on corporate money in politics and U.S. policy toward Israel, but the centrists area also worried that tenants of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), such as abolishing the Senate and prisons, could be used by the GOP to bludgeon Democrats as the ab-normal party.

Appearing on MSNOW’s Morning Joe on Monday, Rahm Emanuel, the former White House chief of staff to President Obama who is considering a run for president in 2028 sought to distance himself — and the Democratic Party itself — from the DSA.

“You’re a separate party,” Emanuel said on the program. “You’re not a caucus or a wing of the party…We’re not open to being taken over.”

“You think people want defunding the police, open borders, opening up the prison doors, I’ll see you in November,” Emanuel continued. “The only way to win is turning red to blue, not blue to midnight blue or cobalt blue.

“You want to get a minimum wage? Red to blue. You want to expand ACA healthcare and get back premium support for working and middle-class families who live paycheck to paycheck? Red to blue,” he added.

Republican strategist Susan Del Percio, who does not support Trump or the MAGA movement, said Emanuel’s tack was the right one, particularly as Democrats fight to make the reasonability case.

“Candidates absolutely need to realign themselves with normal but it’s not enough to be ‘normal.’ You gotta push back on the DSA because no matter how normal the Democrats position themselves, it’ll never be good enough for the voter if the voter associates the Democratic Party with the DSA.”

“And the only one who is doing that is Rahm Emanuel, and he’s doing it well,” she said.

But one Democratic strategist pushed back on the notion that the party should be setting a dividing line at a time when it’s rebuilding and gaining trust from voters.

This source noted that it is the Democratic establishment that has an image problem.

“To a lot of folks in the Democratic Party, the ideologues tend to be the ones who are a little more pure, and have less complications,” the strategist said. “People prefer them to Chuck Schumers and the status quo.”

“We tested out ‘normal’ in 2020 with Joe Biden and that’s not actually what people want,” the strategist added. “I think people romanticize that.”

Others say going normal in 2028 is the best route for the party.

A Democratic donor who spoke to The Hill said if candidates want to win in 2028, they will want “to stand up the most normal candidate” against the Republican nominee.

“The candidate who is the most normal and reasonable will win,” the donor predicted. “But it’s going to be the most normal with a twist. That doesn’t mean we’re going to allow Republicans to throw all the punches. The opposite.”

Democratic strategist Anthony Coley said voters want a return to normalcy because they are “frustrated by prices that are too damn high and weary of the constant drumbeat of Trump-driven drama.

“What they want is actually pretty simple: competent, no-bull—- political leaders who say what they’re going to do and then do what they say.”
